commentary.bottom_line: No study in the supplied evidence tests whether offering a documented AI opt-out with a plain-language account of non-optional uses changes patient understanding, trust, access, or safety. Support for R191 rests on twelve listed endorsements, nine of which are commentaries, so health systems adopting it would be acting on expert opinion rather than tested effects.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero document the hazard. Of the twelve listed sources, one is guidance, two are frameworks, and nine are commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not supply an effect estimate, so certainty about benefit or harm cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

Two commentaries raise opt-out in settings involving vulnerable groups, one on remote oral health monitoring and one on AI translation tools, which are often used with patients who have limited English proficiency. Neither reports data, so the literature offers no evidence on whether these patients can understand or use an opt-out.

Several commentaries tie opt-out to keeping access to traditional care without penalty. No supplied study measures whether patients who decline AI still reach a human clinician or receive equal quality of care. Health systems may therefore need to track these outcomes themselves after adoption.

commentary.research_gap: No study measures whether a visible opt-out and a plain-language list of non-optional AI uses improve patient comprehension, uptake of the opt-out, trust, or access to non-AI care. None examines unintended effects such as delays for patients who opt out. Evaluations that compare disclosure formats and record opt-out rates, wait times, and quality of care for patients who decline would begin to fill this gap.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Two commentaries name vulnerable or language-limited patients as a concern. Health systems cannot assume that an opt-out process designed for general populations will be understood or usable by these groups without translated, literacy-appropriate materials and local evaluation.
